content: Paracoccidioidomycosis, also referred to as Lutz-Splendore-de-Almeida disease or Brazilian blastomycosis, is a fungal infection caused by the thermally dimorphic fungi Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and Paracoccidioides lutzii. This disease is sometimes called South American blastomycosis, but it is caused by a different fungal species than the one responsible for blastomycosis. It is a prevalent mycotic infection in South and Central America. The natural habitat of the infectious agent remains unknown, though it is suspected to be aquatic. Histologically, the fungus appears as a yeast with multiple budding structures, resembling a pilot's wheel. The disease was first identified in 1908 by Adolfo Lutz, a Brazilian physician. In 1912, Luigi Splendore, another Brazilian physician, described the fungus and renamed it Zimonema brasiliense. Later, in 1930, Floriano de Almeida established the genus Paracoccidioides to classify the species and distinguish it from Coccidioides immitis. Paracoccidioidomycosis can be classified based on Franco et al.'s 1987 criteria into four categories: paracoccidioidomycosis infection, paracoccidioidomycosis disease, paracoccidioidomycosis associated with immunosuppression, and residual forms (sequelae). Based on symptom duration, the disease can be further categorized into acute, subacute, or chronic forms. The chronic form is subdivided into unifocal and multifocal presentations. The primary mode of infection is through the inhalation of fungal spores from Paracoccidioides brasiliensis, which grow in the soil of endemic rural areas. Differential diagnoses for the acute form of paracoccidioidomycosis include lymphoma, leukemia, toxoplasmosis, and sarcoidosis. For the chronic form, differential diagnoses include tuberculosis, leishmaniasis, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, cryptococcosis, actinomycosis, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis, squamous cell carcinoma, and Wegener's granulomatosis. Paracoccidioidomycosis is endemic in South and Central America, predominantly affecting agricultural workers. The countries with the highest prevalence are Brazil, Argentina, and Venezuela, with Brazil reporting the majority of cases. The disease is more common in men than women, though anyone can be affected. Risk factors for developing paracoccidioidomycosis include poor hygiene, malnutrition, smoking, and alcohol consumption. In endemic rural areas, children may become infected but typically do not develop the disease until later in life. As they age, the disease may manifest.
